title: He Painted This Flower Market and His Bleakest Beach Scene the Same Week, on Panels Almost the Same Size.
standfirst: In September 1885 James McNeill Whistler spent a few days in Dieppe and brought home two tiny pictures now kept a short walk apart in a Washington gallery: this cheerful watercolour of a market, and an oil of an empty, grey beach that is almost its exact twin in scale. He gave this one to his host as a keepsake. Eleven years later he stood in court testifying against him.

sections.heading: Two Pictures, One Week, Almost One Size
sections.body: In September 1885 Whistler travelled to Dieppe to see his pupil Walter Sickert and Sickert's new wife, and the two men [painted together](https://whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/biog/?nid=SickW) during the stay, working at times from the same models. At least two pictures survive from that visit, and they could not be more different in mood. This watercolour shows women browsing flower stalls under striped awnings, ["exuberant, full of bright light,"](https://publications.asia.si.edu/whistler-in-watercolor/object-curatorial-analysis.php?q=3391) built from clashing, happy blues and oranges. The other, Grey and Brown: The Sad Sea Shore, is an oil on wood panel showing an almost empty beach in flat brown sand and grey sea, with [no horizon visible at all](https://www.whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/printdisplay/?mid=y330) — unique, in the cataloguer's words, among everything else Whistler painted. The two pictures are also nearly the same object: this one measures 12.8 by 21 centimetres, the beach scene 12.5 by 21.7 — a few millimetres apart in each direction. Both ended up, by different routes, in the Freer Gallery of Art. Whistler could paint the same stretch of French coast as pure cheer or as a complaint, within the same handful of days, on panels cut to almost the same size.

sections.heading: The Pupil Who Got It as a Gift
sections.body: Walter Sickert met Whistler in 1879 while a student at the Slade School of Art, left the school in 1882, and spent most of the 1880s as Whistler's [pupil and studio assistant](https://whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/biog/?nid=SickW). A letter Sickert later wrote fixes [the date of the gift](https://publications.asia.si.edu/whistler-in-watercolor/object-curatorial-analysis.php?q=3391) to that September 1885 stay in Dieppe — Whistler gave it to him directly, during the visit. Looking back decades later, the Hunterian's own catalogue judged that of everyone who worked alongside Whistler, Sickert "probably understood [Whistler's aims and achievements](https://whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/biog/?nid=SickW) more than any other artist" — a line that reads, in hindsight, like an epitaph for a friendship that would not survive to the next decade intact.

sections.heading: A Farthing, a Bankruptcy, and a New Trade in Small Pictures
sections.body: Seven years before Dieppe, Whistler had sued the critic John Ruskin for libel after Ruskin wrote that his Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket was worth [flinging a pot of paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_McNeill_Whistler) in the public's face. Whistler won the case in November 1878 and was awarded a farthing, with the court costs split between them; the farthing covered nothing, and by May 1879 he had been declared bankrupt, his house and its contents sold at auction. He rebuilt on watercolour, a medium he had barely taken seriously before a commissioned set of Venice etchings turned into fourteen months of unusual productivity in 1879 and 1880. He later described the resulting watercolours, pastels and small oils as ["a wonderful game"](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/hidden-more-eight-decades-these-exquisite-watercolors-james-mcneill-whistler-make-their-public-debut-180972341/) — small, quick, and aimed at the wealthy American tourists then touring Europe. The Dieppe flower market, six years later, is one more round of that same game.

sections.heading: The Fruiterer He Still Owed Money To
sections.body: That same summer, Whistler found another small, saleable subject closer to home, and the story of how survives almost as a piece of theatre. Riding in a cab with the painter William Merritt Chase, he spotted a greengrocer's shop at a Chelsea corner, had the cabby circle it from several angles, and finally said, ["Isn't it beautiful?"](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/13973/pg13973-images.html) — "I believe I'll have that crate of oranges moved over there, against that background of green. Yes, that's better," he added, and settled back contentedly. The shop belonged to George Terrey, at 45 Cheyne Walk — and Terrey had been one of Whistler's creditors seven years earlier, owed more than £20 he had no way to pay when the bankruptcy proceedings opened. Terrey's Fruit Shop, Chelsea, the watercolour that resulted, is dated to [1885 or 1886](https://www.whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/printdisplay/?mid=m1002). Nothing in the record says whether the debt itself was ever settled. What the record does show is a bankrupt painter turning his own unpaid grocer's bill into stock for sale.

sections.heading: A Lecture That Argued Against Painting Things as They Were
sections.body: Seven months before Dieppe, on 20 February 1885, Whistler had stood on a London stage and argued against the very thing both this watercolour and the Terrey shop do. In the lecture now known as the Ten O'Clock, he told his audience that the idea ["Nature is always right"](https://archive.org/stream/mrwhistlerstenoc00whis/mrwhistlerstenoc00whis_djvu.txt) was "an assertion, artistically, as untrue, as it is one whose truth is universally taken for granted," and that nature supplied only raw material — the keyboard contains the notes of all music — for an artist to [pick, and choose, and group](https://archive.org/stream/mrwhistlerstenoc00whis/mrwhistlerstenoc00whis_djvu.txt) into something nature itself had never arranged. He had been making some version of that argument since the 1860s, which is also why, in 1874, he turned down Edgar Degas's invitation to [show with the first Impressionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_McNeill_Whistler): he wanted tonal harmony built in the studio, not a faithful record of a passing moment. The crate of oranges he had a cabby move for a better view makes the same point in miniature. The record behind this page still files the flower market as Impressionism anyway. It reads, in spirit, closer to the plain, unarranged subject his own lecture had just finished arguing a painter should never settle for.

sections.heading: The Friendship the Gift Outlasted by Eleven Years
sections.body: Whatever this watercolour marked between the two men did not last. On 12 October 1896, Sickert failed to apologise to Whistler for siding with Sir William Eden during Whistler's legal dispute with Eden over a portrait commission, and the two [became estranged](https://whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/biog/?nid=SickW). The breach widened the following year: when the writer Joseph Pennell sued Sickert for libel over an article on lithography, Whistler appeared as [Pennell's principal witness](https://whistlerpaintings.gla.ac.uk/catalogue/biog/?nid=SickW) against the pupil who had once painted beside him on a Dieppe beach. Grey and Brown: The Sad Sea Shore reached the Freer Gallery in 1914, eleven years after Whistler's death. Flower Market: Dieppe had already left Sickert's hands and passed through the London dealer Obach & Co. by the time [Freer bought it in 1907](https://publications.asia.si.edu/whistler-in-watercolor/object-curatorial-analysis.php?q=3391) — sold on, by whatever route, well before the friendship that produced it was over.
